item.title: University students’ overreliance on generative AI feedback in the learning process: the effects of perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and metacognitive monitoring
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has introduced an important question in education, when AI provides immediate and reliable feedback, do students use it as a learning support tool or gradually rely on it as a substitute for their own cognitive efforts? Drawing on Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Offloading Theory, and Metacognitive Monitoring Theory, this study develops a theoretical model to explain the formation process of undergraduate students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Specifically, this study examines the relationships among perceived cognitive load, cognitive offloading, and overreliance on GAI feedback, while further exploring how metacognitive monitoring levels shape this process. A questionnaire survey was conducted among 600 undergraduate students, and structural equation modeling was performed using AMOS 31.0. The results showed that perceived cognitive load significantly and positively predicted cognitive offloading, which further contributed to students’ overreliance on GAI feedback. Meanwhile, perceived cognitive load also directly predicted overreliance on GAI feedback. Bootstrap analysis further confirmed that cognitive offloading mediated the relationship between perceived cognitive load and overreliance on GAI feedback. In addition, this study established separate structural equation models for students with different levels of metacognitive monitoring and found distinct patterns in the formation of GAI feedback overreliance. Specifically, students with lower metacognitive monitoring were more likely to be influenced by cognitive pressure during learning, showing a more prominent direct relationship between perceived cognitive load and GAI feedback overreliance. This finding suggests that these students tend to rely more directly on GAI feedback when facing higher cognitive demands. In contrast, students with higher metacognitive monitoring demonstrated a more evident cognitive regulation process, in which cognitive offloading played a more important role in linking perceived cognitive load with GAI feedback overreliance. This indicates that these students may actively adjust their cognitive resource allocation when using GAI, although continuous cognitive offloading may still increase their dependence on AI-generated feedback.

item.title: Psychological pathways to responsible generative AI decision-making among teachers: governance clarity, perceived accountability, decision uncertainty, and AI literacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can assist teachers with organizing information, generating alternatives, and drafting feedback. Its use in consequential judgments requires verifiable evidence and professional oversight. This study examines how teachers regulate optional GenAI assistance while preserving professional judgment. Methods Research on felt accountability, metacognitive monitoring, and AI literacy is conceptually integrated to develop a psychological process model of teacher decision episodes. Governance clarity is specified through rule clarity and role clarity, with responsible GenAI decision-making defined as regulated decision conduct. Results The conceptual analysis produces five testable propositions and one configurational expectation. Governance clarity is proposed to support responsible conduct through perceived accountability. Decision uncertainty is modeled as a metacognitive signal whose behavioral value depends on calibration and regulation; AI literacy is specified as a resource for verification, calibrated reliance, and appropriate escalation. Responsible conduct encompasses appropriate delegation, verification, calibrated reliance and accountable human authority, traceability, and escalation or override. These model outputs are theoretical propositions, not empirically established effects. Discussion The framework distinguishes generative assistance from conventional algorithmic advice and identifies task-dependent applications in assessment, feedback, referral, and student support. Future tests should compare unaided and assisted judgment, distinguish process quality from decision accuracy, and examine stakes, reversibility, and contextual dependence. Teachers retain authority to accept, modify, or reject GenAI output, or proceed without GenAI assistance.

item.title: Generative AI and student motivation: an SDT-guided systematic review of learning activities, motivational regulation, and measurement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The application of Generative AI is reshaping students’ learning. However, student motivation in GenAI-supported learning is complex and influenced by multiple factors. To fully realize the educational potential of GenAI, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between student motivation and GenAI is necessary. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review examined 39 articles published between 2023 and 2025, drawn from two databases: Web of Science and Scopus. This study provides three major findings. First, competence-related learning activities were the most frequently identified across the reviewed studies. Second, four categories were reported in relation to student motivation: GenAI characteristics, learner factors, psychological factors, and environmental factors. Third, three major aspects of motivational conceptualization are basic psychological needs, motivation construct, and motivation-related construct. In addition, quantitative questionnaires were the dominant approach used to measure these constructs. Finally, the relationship among these three findings is illustrated. The findings provide insights into student motivation in GenAI-supported learning and highlight the relevance of GenAI characteristics, learners, and the learning environment. This study also provides theoretical and practical implications for facilitating students’ motivation in GenAI-supported learning environments.

item.title: Metacognitive disengagement and knowledge innovation quality in human–AI collaboration: the mediating role of cognitive offloading and the moderating roles of task complexity and AI literacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the cognitive conditions of knowledge innovation. While human–AI collaboration improves the efficiency of knowledge production, it may also induce creators to outsourcing cognitive work to AI systems. This study conceptualized this tendency as task-level metacognitive disengagement, defined as the immediate reduction of planning, monitoring, and reflection within a specific AI-assisted task, and, drawing on metacognition theory, cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory, examined its impact on knowledge innovation quality, its psychological mechanism, and boundary conditions through four complementary experiments. Experiment 1 showed that higher AI assistance significantly increased metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 2 revealed that cognitive offloading partially mediated the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 3 confirmed the negative effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality, specifically on novelty, usefulness, and developability, with metacognitive disengagement partially mediating this effect. Experiment 4 tested the proposed moderated mediation model and found that task complexity strengthened, whereas individual AI literacy weakened, the negative indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. These findings reveal a hidden cognitive cost behind the efficiency gains of human–AI collaboration and provide empirical evidence and theoretical implications for cultivating innovative talent and designing human–AI collaborative mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

item.title: AI literacy and vocational students’ complex problem-solving skills: a moderated mediation model of systematic thinking, cognitive load, and perceived school ICT support
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
As technological advancements such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshape the landscape of work, career development in vocational education is increasingly oriented toward dynamic, long-term personal growth. In this context, Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) have become a critical competence, reflecting students’ capacity to address ill-structured tasks and adapt to rapidly changing environments. Grounded in Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines the relationship between AI Literacy and students’ self-reported Complex Problem-Solving Skills (CPS) in higher vocational colleges and the cognitive pathways that may help explain this relationship. This study posits that AI Literacy, as a personal agentic factor, is positively associated with self-reported CPS both directly and indirectly through Systematic Thinking Skills and cognitive load, and that perceived school information and communication technology (ICT) support may condition the strength of these associations. To provide temporal separation among the focal measures, a multi-wave survey was administered to 784 students from six higher vocational institutions at three time points. Data were analyzed using SPSS and Mplus. Results indicated that AI Literacy was significantly associated with self-reported CPS, with significant indirect effects estimated through Systematic Thinking Skills and the six-item cognitive-load composite. Notably, the associations between AI Literacy and these cognitive factors were stronger at higher levels of perceived school ICT support. These findings highlight the relevance of AI Literacy and students’ perceptions of ICT support to self-reported CPS and their preparation for AI-integrated workplaces.

item.title: Learning engagement and creative self-beliefs in generative AI-supported design education: self-reported prompt literacy and dimensions of AI dependence
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI (GenAI) is changing how design students learn, yet little is known about how students’ perceived capability to work with GenAI relates to their learning engagement and motivational self-beliefs, or under which forms of AI dependence this link is weaker. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this cross-sectional study examined self-reported prompt literacy, learning engagement, and two components of the creative self: creative self-efficacy (CSE), a motivational belief in one’s creative capability, and creative personal identity (CPI), the importance of creativity to one’s self-concept. Survey data came from 829 undergraduate art and design students in 40 intact classes at two institutions in mainland China; latent-variable and moderation models accounted for the clustering of students within classes. Self-reported prompt literacy was positively associated with engagement ( β = 0.54), and engagement was positively associated with both CSE ( β = 0.62) and CPI ( β = 0.47). Engagement was more strongly associated with CSE than with CPI (difference = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24]) and remained uniquely associated with CPI after CSE was taken into account. When four dimensions of AI dependence were modeled simultaneously, the prompt literacy–engagement association was weaker among students reporting higher cognitive dependence; evidence for loss of control was weaker, and functional and emotional dependence showed no clear unique moderation. All interaction effects were small. The dimensional analysis identified cognitive dependence as the clearest moderator. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings suggest possible boundary conditions for the capability–engagement association and require longitudinal and behavioral testing.

item.title: Behavioral and psychosocial indicators for depression and anxiety risk stratification among college students: development and external validation of a machine-learning-assisted framework
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Depression and anxiety symptoms are common among college students. Behavioral and psychosocial indicators may support preventive campus mental health work, but risk-stratification frameworks require external validation. Methods We developed a construct-level model-explanation framework using questionnaire data from a development sample. The cleaned dataset included 1,267 students; internal-validation analyses included 1,096 students for depression risk and 1,095 for anxiety risk. Risk was defined as a Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) or Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7 (GAD-7) score of 10 or higher. The primary Feature set C random-forest (RF) pipelines integrated demographic, traditional, and emerging behavioral and psychosocial indicators. Fold-specific preprocessing and percentile cutoffs were used for internal validation. Locked pipelines were applied without retraining, predictor reselection, optimization, recalibration, or threshold adjustment to an independent university sample of 1,468 students. Results External area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), area under the precision–recall curve (PR-AUC), and Brier scores were 0.813 (95% CI, 0.776–0.848), 0.402 (0.325–0.491), and 0.090 (0.083–0.098), respectively, for depression and 0.809 (0.765–0.851), 0.205 (0.144–0.300), and 0.063 (0.056–0.070), respectively, for anxiety. Ordinary participant-level bootstrap was the primary approach, with stratified bootstrap as a sensitivity analysis. Depression calibration was close to the prevalence baseline (Brier 0.091; intercept −0.668; slope 1.401), whereas anxiety showed miscalibration (Brier 0.063 vs. baseline 0.051; intercept −1.227; slope 1.102). The models supported external discrimination and risk ranking but did not validate individual absolute-risk probabilities or clinical thresholds. Conclusion Behavioral and psychosocial indicators supported externally validated risk stratification in an independent university sample. Anxiety-risk findings should be interpreted as preliminary because the number of positive cases was limited. Further evaluation is needed before wider implementation.

item.title: The association between large language model dependence and academic anxiety among nursing students: statistical indirect associations through artificial intelligence addiction and academic burnout
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Increasing use of large language models in nursing education has raised questions about the association between reliance on these tools and academic distress. This study examined direct and specific indirect associations between large language model dependence (LMD) and academic anxiety (AA) through artificial intelligence addiction (AIA) and academic burnout (AB). Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from March to April 2026 among 473 nursing students in Guangdong Province, China, including students undertaking clinical placements. The four constructs were assessed using items selected from published self-report instruments. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was performed with age and sex included as covariates. Direct and specific indirect associations were evaluated using bootstrapping with 5,000 resamples. Results Cronbach’s α ranged from 0.914 to 0.944, composite reliability from 0.935 to 0.954, and average variance extracted from 0.560 to 0.721. Heterotrait–monotrait ratios ranged from 0.485 to 0.733, supporting discriminant validity. Model fit evidence was mixed: SRMR was 0.068, whereas NFI was 0.812, below the 0.90 reference value. The model explained 49.2% of the variance in academic anxiety. Large language model dependence showed a small positive direct association with academic anxiety ( β = 0.138, 95% CI [0.006, 0.278], p = 0.048). Significant specific indirect associations were identified through academic burnout ( β = 0.205, 95% CI [0.123, 0.303]) and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout ( β = 0.098, 95% CI [0.049, 0.147]); both p < 0.001. Conclusion Large language model dependence was positively associated with academic anxiety among nursing students, with specific indirect associations through academic burnout and through artificial intelligence addiction followed by academic burnout. These findings highlight the relevance of problematic AI use and study-related exhaustion to academic distress. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering or causal mediation.

item.title: Development and validation of the AI cognitive offloading scale for Chinese college students
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Against the backdrop of rapid advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI), college students increasingly delegate cognitive tasks to AI systems. This study developed and validated the AI Cognitive Offloading Scale (AI-COS) as an alternative, context-specific operationalization for Chinese college students, focusing on the cognitive functions delegated to AI during learning. Methods An initial pool of 26 items was generated through literature review, theoretical analysis, and expert evaluation. Study 1 used data from 665 college students for item analysis and exploratory factor analysis. Study 2 used an independent sample of 1,123 college students for confirmatory factor analysis, reliability testing, criterion-related validity assessment, and measurement invariance testing across gender. Results Exploratory factor analysis yielded a 20-item scale with three dimensions: memory offloading, assistive offloading, and thinking offloading. The second-order three-factor model showed satisfactory fit (CFI = 0.951, TLI = 0.944, RMSEA = 0.047, SRMR = 0.036). The scale demonstrated strong internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.944), split-half reliability (0.932), and test-retest reliability (0.937). Convergent validity was satisfactory, and full scalar invariance across gender was reported. The total score and all three dimensions were positively associated with AI dependence and negatively associated with metacognitive monitoring. The total score and assistive offloading were negatively associated with need for cognition, whereas memory and thinking offloading were not significantly associated with need for cognition. Discussion The findings provide initial evidence for the reliability and validity of the AI-COS. The three dimensions represent distinguishable functions of cognitive delegation rather than a developmental sequence. The scale offers a context-specific instrument for research on AI-mediated cognition, learning regulation, and student development.

item.title: Changes in Perceptions of Trust in Human-AI Interactions
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
This study examined how educational briefings about Artificial Intelligence (AI) hallucinations influence user trust, caution, and willingness to continue using AI systems. We recruited 51 participants through the online platform Prolific for an online questionnaire evaluating AI use and task-focused AI scenarios. After questions about trust and AI, participants read about common inaccuracies in Large Language Models. Participants showed a significant decrease in self-reported trust, indicating increased awareness of AI limitations. Contrary to expectations, perceptions of AI reliability and competence did not predict willingness to reuse AI in academic scenarios. Affective trust played a stronger role than cognitive trust, with perceived emotional support significantly predicting forgiveness of AI errors. Increased caution also predicted greater recalibration of trust, although willingness to continue using AI remained high. These findings suggest that educational interventions can promote calibrated trust in AI without discouraging continued use, highlighting the importance of transparency and context-sensitive design.

item.title: When Generative AI Helps and Hurts: Augmentation-Substitution Taxonomy and Recovery Pattern in University Students’ Experiences
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative AI is now widely used in higher education, yet the same tool can produce positive and negative outcomes for the same user, and the reasons for this remain underexplored. Using technology affordance theory, this study develops an empirically grounded taxonomy of interaction mechanisms based on students’ retrospective accounts. The 71 participants, who began university after the public release of generative AI, completed surveys and reported 254 experiences through interviews and written reflections. Three key findings emerged: first, most students reported both positive and negative experiences, with no measured person-level trait robustly associated with experiential valence; second, 17 interaction mechanisms were identified, organized by whether AI complemented or replaced cognitive tasks; third, some students shifted from negative to more positive trajectories. Experiential valence thus appears more closely associated with interaction context than with person-level traits, although the evidence is retrospective rather than causal.

item.title: Generative artificial intelligence reshapes university students' sustainable use of academic information resources: mixed evidence from behavioral logs and perceptual survey data
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students retrieve and consume academic information, yet whether it substitutes for or complements library resources remains contested, and prior surveys rarely separate auxiliary from substitutive use. Methods This study uses a convergent triangulation design that combines multiple quantitative methods. It addresses the same set of research propositions by collecting perceptual-level questionnaire data and behavioral-level logs and platform usage statistics, analyzing them independently, and comparing the findings at the interpretation stage. Using 368 student questionnaires, we test an auxiliary-substitutive dual-path structural equation model and compare the results with an interrupted time-series analysis of 3.2 million print-loan logs (2017-2025) and digital-platform statistics from 2021 to the first half of 2026. Results Print-resource continuance intention is positively associated with deep-reading demand, but not significantly associated with auxiliary GenAI use. Survey results showed auxiliary GenAI use positively associated with digital-resource continuance intention, yet insufficiently distinct from perceived digital-resource convenience; platform data showed nascent use of embedded AI features. Substitutive GenAI use shows only a weak negative association with print-resource continuance intention, while the nine-year loan record reveals no significant level or trend change at the January 2023 breakpoint; task-channel fit shows no significant moderating effect. Discussion In this institution, findings align more with dual-channel coexistence than with the “AI-replaces-libraries” narrative; the survey-level substitution association has not yet appeared in aggregate borrowing behavior, informing collection development, service redesign, and AI-literacy education.

item.title: How much can music listening habits tell us about mental health? An interpretable machine learning benchmark using genre preference and self-reported anxiety, depression, insomnia, and obsessive–compulsive symptoms
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Music listening is widely believed to index mental health, and this belief underwrites applications inferring psychological state from listening records. We estimated how much information musical preference and listening behavior carry about self-reported distress, and tested whether classification accuracy reported for a widely reused public dataset reflects discriminative skill or class imbalance. Methods Cross-sectional secondary analysis of the Music and Mental Health (MxMH) survey ( n = 736), a self-selected online convenience sample collected in 2022 with no probability sampling frame, no design weights, and no measurement of gender, geography, education, income, or clinical history. In total, 42 predictors covering genre exposure, favorite genre, streaming platform, listening hours, tempo preference, and musical engagement were modeled against four single-item, unvalidated self-anchored distress ratings, a secondary composite index, and a self-attributed judgment of whether music improves mental health. Elastic net, support vector machine, random forest, and gradient boosting models were compared against mean-prediction and majority-class baselines using nested cross-validation, corrected t -tests, permutation nulls, and Shapley additive explanations. Results Out-of-sample explanatory power was small. Random forests achieved cross-validated R 2 values of 0.068 for depression, 0.058 for the composite index, 0.032 for anxiety, and 0.006 or below for insomnia and obsessive–compulsive ratings, exceeding the mean-prediction baseline for all outcomes except insomnia ( p = 0.157). Permutation tests separated depression, anxiety, the composite, and obsessive–compulsive ratings from noise, but not insomnia ( p = 0.198). For the self-attributed effect of music, the best classifier reached 74.7% accuracy against a majority-class baseline of 74.5% ( p = 0.896), while balanced accuracy peaked at 0.551 and the Matthews correlation coefficient at 0.135. Conclusion Listening habits carry a real but very small signal about self-reported distress, and apparent accuracy on this dataset is an artifact of class imbalance. Musical preference is not a usable individual-level marker of psychological state. These estimates come from a single, heavily reused, non-representative convenience sample with unvalidated single-item outcomes and no demographic weighting variables, so they characterize this archive rather than any defined population and require independent replication before any specific effect size is treated as settled. Dataset: MxMH survey, Kaggle.

item.title: Baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and AI avatars
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
People routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. The present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. Across three experiments with Chinese university students (total N = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (Experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (Experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (AI) avatar designs (Experiment 3). Participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. The results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. These findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of AI systems.

item.title: Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in the AI era: a longitudinal reflexive thematic analysis of teacher reflective journals
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Objective Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) lowers the threshold for producing work, not necessarily for learning. This study examines how an instructor kept an interdisciplinary AI course teachable for first-year art students, where that effort reached its limits, and how the instructor interpreted students' engagement with AI tools. Methods The study is a longitudinal practitioner self-study of a 12-week course taught in autumn 2025 at a higher vocational college in northwestern China. The data are the instructor's own reflective journals: structured entries written during the semester for Weeks 1–7 and retrospective accounts of Weeks 8–12 written after the semester ended. The two strata are reported separately. Reflexive thematic analysis produced 40 evidence anchors, five themes, one cross-cutting thread, and one central organizing theme, with a full audit trail. Results The instructor's repairs (translating content into everyday and discipline-specific tasks, working around broken or restricted lab equipment, and demonstrating on the teacher's computer) kept the course running. However, as content moved toward frontier tools that required paid accounts, computing resources, and prior AI experience, teaching drifted toward demonstration (“the more cutting-edge something is, the more it can only be demonstrated”). Across the semester the instructor recorded a recurring pattern, here termed a teacher-perceived low-threshold illusion , in which students appeared, in the instructor's account, to treat seeing, bookmarking, or one-click generation as equivalent to being able to do. The instructor associated this pattern with three co-occurring conditions: natural-language prompting and one-click generation, demonstration-only teaching, and a final assessment that students could complete without having attended. Participation could be high while, in the instructor's judgement, students gained little. Conclusion Pedagogical resilience reconstruction in AI teaching is bounded. Keeping an AI course running did not by itself make learning visible: the journals record a tension between engagement, product completion, and evidence of learning, not an established failure of learning. In-course repair reached limits shaped by access conditions and an inherited assessment format, and reconstruction of the course took place at the scale of the semester. We present pedagogical resilience reconstruction as an emerging construct for multi-case testing.

item.title: Who benefits from LLMs? Prompt engineering competence and equity in higher education
item.description:
International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are rapidly becoming embedded in higher education, yet their benefits may be unevenly distributed. This study conceptualizes prompt engineering competence (PEC) as an equity-relevant interaction competence and examines whether differences in PEC are associated with perceived academic gains and perceived educational inequity. We adopt a two-stage quantitative design combining a cross-sectional survey with a within-subject prompt-quality experiment. Stage 1 reports a survey of Chinese undergraduates who have used LLMs ( N = 380), measuring PEC, perceived academic performance gains, perceived educational inequity, family digital capital, gaming experience, and a planning/independent-work tendency. Regression and mediation analyses show that PEC was strongly associated with perceived academic gains, while its association with perceived inequity was statistically significant but small. Background resources and learning-related experiences and dispositions explained substantial variance in PEC, especially gaming experience and planning/independent-work tendency, and the association between family digital capital and perceived academic gains was largely indirect through PEC. Stage 2 conducts a within-subject prompt-quality experiment across four higher-education task types and four popular models, comparing basic prompts with a student-oriented five-component refined prompt framework (Role–Goal–Input–Process–Output). Analysis of 400 matched prompt comparisons, comprising 800 model outputs, indicates that the refined prompt scaffold consistently outperforms basic prompts. Overall, the findings identify PEC as a potential competence pathway through which students may differ in their ability to convert LLM access into learning-related benefits, while structured prompt scaffolds may provide a scalable approach to reducing prompt-quality barriers in LLM-supported higher education.

item.title: Beyond trustworthiness: Psychological and institutional drivers of university students' AI chatbot adoption in Vietnam
item.description:
Acta Psychologica
Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in higher education, but it remains unclear whether factors associated with perceived trustworthiness are also associated with students' intentions to adopt them. Drawing on an extended UTAUT2 framework, this study examines how chatbot-specific attributes are associated with trustworthiness, performance expectancy, and hedonic motivation, and how these appraisals, together with UTAUT2 factors, relate to behavioral intention. Survey data from 604 university students in Vietnam were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that ethics (β = 0.294, p < .001) and design (β = 0.458, p < .001) were positively associated with perceived trustworthiness, while social influence was not. Design and interactivity were positively associated with performance expectancy and hedonic motivation. However, perceived trustworthiness (β = 0.043, p = .153), hedonic motivation, and effort expectancy were not significantly associated with behavioral intention. Instead, behavioral intention was most strongly associated with price value (β = 0.408, p < .001), performance expectancy (β = 0.281, p < .001), social influence, and facilitating conditions, and was strongly associated with students' self-reported continued-use tendency (β = 0.754, p < .001). Perceived trustworthiness was not independently associated with behavioral intention in the present model, whereas price value and performance expectancy showed the largest positive associations with intention. This pattern highlights the value of considering trustworthiness alongside instrumental, social, and institutional evaluations when explaining AI-chatbot adoption. The study extends UTAUT2 by integrating these adoption evaluations with an assurance-oriented appraisal of the AI system.

item.title: Student Engagement and Trust Calibration With Generative AI in a 5S Safety Assessment
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Generative AI is increasingly used in engineering and technology education, but its role in safety education remains underexplored. This study examined undergraduate students’ ( N = 14) human-AI interaction during a 5S workplace safety assessment in a Human Factors course. Using a mixed-methods design, we analyzed User Engagement Scale–Short Form (UES-SF) responses and qualitative reflections after students independently completed a hazard identification task and compared findings with a parallel AI-generated assessment (ChatGPT-4o). Results revealed high perceived reward and value, minimal usability barriers, and mixed focused attention, suggesting task engagement without deep immersion. Qualitatively, students described AI as expanding hazard awareness, improving analytical structure, and accelerating information retrieval, while consistently emphasizing the necessity of human oversight and cautioning against overreliance. Integrated findings position generative AI as a human-in-the-loop decision-support tool: effective for scaffolding systematic reasoning and broadening hazard recognition, but insufficient as a substitute for domain-informed judgment.

item.title: Human Factors Extended Reality Showcase 2026
item.description:
Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
Extended reality (XR) technologies are increasingly adopted by human factors researchers and practitioners across domains ranging from manufacturing to workplace safety and ergonomics. This interactive XR Showcase session provides attendees with direct, hands-on engagement with XR devices and applications presented by researchers. This year’s demonstrations reflect growing interest in XR applications for skilled manual work and assembly, workplace safety and ergonomics, visualization, and mobility interaction. While training remains an established theme, an emerging trend is the integration of artificial intelligence within XR. Collectively, these demonstrations illustrate a broader shift in the field toward XR platforms that serve not only as visualization tools, but as integrated systems for performance measurement and human-AI collaboration. The XR Showcase advances the goals of HFES by strengthening community interaction and facilitating knowledge exchange among researchers, practitioners, and students interested in the expanding role of XR in human factors research and practice.

item.title: The use of AI chatbot on efl students’ speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate: through the lens of activity theory
item.description:
BMC Psychology
English as a foreign language (EFL) educators have increasingly incorporated Artificial Intelligence (AI) into language learning; accordingly, this study explored the role of an AI-supported speaking tool in speaking skills, speaking anxiety, and willingness to communicate (WTC) among Chinese EFL students. Activity theory refers to a proper and applicable structure proposed for investigating how AI chatbots affect different dimensions. Applying this theory to the research allows for analyzing the complicated interactions between those factors and a comprehension of the effect of AI chatbots (EAP Talk) on learners’ WTC, speaking proficiency, and speaking anxiety. A total of 113 participants were initially recruited (58 EG, 55 CG); after excluding four multivariate outliers (all from the EG), the primary analytic sample comprised 109 learners (54 EG, 55 CG). Full-sample results ( N = 113) are also reported and were consistent in direction, though smaller in magnitude for speaking anxiety (see Sensitivity Analysis). Using pretests, the participants’ levels of speaking abilities, anxiety, and WTC were assessed prior to the intervention. Subsequently, the EG received AI-supported speaking practice through EAP Talk, an AI-based speaking assessment and feedback application that facilitated iterative practice and immediate automated feedback, whereas the CG was taught the same material without the use of this tool. Using post-tests following the treatment, both groups were evaluated on their speaking skills, anxiety, and WTC. The results revealed notable posttest differences between the two groups: WTC showed a medium effect size, speaking anxiety showed a large effect size, and speaking skill showed a very large effect size. Overall, the results suggest that the EAP Talk intervention was associated with improved speaking performance and WTC, as well as reduced speaking anxiety among the participating EFL students. Interpreting the findings through the lens of Activity Theory helps situate the results within the broader relationships among learners, tools, and instructional context; however, the theory is used here as an interpretive lens rather than as a directly tested explanatory model.

item.title: Toward an Interpretive Synthesis of Personalization, Co-Design, and Ethical Mediation in AI-Supported Higher Education: An Integrative Review of Agentic, Generative, and Adaptive Tutoring Systems
item.description:
Journal of Educational Computing Research
Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and adaptive learning technologies are expanding in higher education, raising questions about their alignment with pedagogical goals. This qualitative-integrative review synthesizes 57 publications (21 empirical, 25 conceptual or framework, 9 systematic reviews or meta-analyses retained for triangulation, and 2 design/development papers) from 2024 to 2026, employing Whittemore and Knafl’s methodology to examine AI-supported tutoring, implementation strategies, and learner/instructor experiences. Three interpretive themes organize this heterogeneous evidence: (1) personalization as a recurring target, from micro-level adaptation to curriculum design; (2) technology-pedagogy co-design as a recurring implementation pattern; and (3) contextual and ethical conditions surrounding adoption, including culture, policy gaps, well-being, and academic integrity. These themes are interpretive, not a validated framework, and draw on evidence of uneven strength. The present review does not estimate effect sizes or pool outcomes across studies; g = 0.70, reported by X. Wang et al. in a separate meta-analysis of 45 studies (2010–2022) of pre-generative adaptive systems, which is cited only as background, not as a finding of this review. Implications are framed as evidence-tiered hypotheses, while the layered model is offered as an interpretive scaffold for future research, not a confirmatory model.

item.title: How does community of inquiry matter? Mediating effects and configurational pathways linking project-based learning design to learning engagement
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has reshaped animation students’ skill profiles and the conditions of instructional design in project-based learning (PBL) studios. We examine whether and how perceptions of PBL design are associated with Learning Engagement (LE), treating AIGC-assisted PBL studios as the research context rather than testing generative AI as a model variable. Drawing on Community of Inquiry (CoI) theory, we examine Problem Driven (PD), Project Design (PDe), Project Implementation (PI), and Project Evaluation (PE) as antecedents; Cognitive Presence (CP), Social Presence (SP), and Teaching Presence (TP) as statistical mediators; and LE as the outcome. We analyzed two-wave survey data from 490 upper-year animation students using PLS-SEM and fsQCA. PBL and CoI were measured concurrently at T1, and LE at T2; indirect effects therefore represent indirect statistical associations rather than mediation with a fully established temporal sequence. PD, PDe, and PI showed significant positive direct associations with LE. PE’s zero-order and single-predictor associations were positive, but its direct path coefficient became significantly negative after controlling for the other PBL dimensions and CoI mediators. The coefficient was sensitive to model specification, suggesting possible statistical suppression; it should not be interpreted as evidence that evaluation itself inherently inhibits engagement. The three CoI dimensions showed significant statistical mediation associations across all 12 indirect paths. TP and SP had relatively higher point estimates of indirect statistical associations, but differences between indirect effects were not formally tested; no dimension is claimed to be optimal. PE’s positive indirect associations through CoI partially offset its negative net direct association without reversing the total association after adjustment. The extent of this offset may depend on the degree to which CoI-related experiences are concurrently reported. fsQCA identified seven high-engagement configurations. No individual PBL dimension was indispensable. CoI dimensions appeared as core or peripheral conditions, although not every configuration included all three. These findings clarify the dual pathways linking evaluation and engagement through indirect statistical associations and configurational conditions, and provide guidance for optimizing PBL under different resource constraints. Conclusions are limited to AIGC-assisted PBL studios and do not establish the instructional effects of generative AI.

item.title: Psychological mechanisms of perceived technological dependence on generative artificial intelligence tools: perceived knowledge, trust, anxiety, and self-efficacy
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Generative AI tools are increasingly used in design education, yet the relationship between students’ perceptions of these tools and their reported reliance on them remains unclear. This study analyzed cross-sectional survey responses from 526 undergraduate students in design-related disciplines using partial least squares structural equation modeling. In the specified model, perceived reliability, perceived usefulness, and perceived intelligence were positively associated with perceived AIGC knowledge, whereas perceived ease of use was not significantly associated with it. Perceived AIGC knowledge was positively associated with trust, self-efficacy, and usage intention and negatively associated with AIGC-related anxiety. Trust, AIGC-related anxiety, and self-efficacy each showed a significant indirect effect in the modeled relationship between perceived AIGC knowledge and usage intention. Usage intention was strongly associated with perceived technological dependence. These findings are consistent with the proposed framework, but the cross-sectional data do not establish the temporal sequence of the constructs or show that reported dependence reflects harmful overuse. The study extends technology acceptance research by examining perceived reliance in AIGC-supported creative work.

item.title: Twenty-Five Years, Five Projects, and Five Reflections on Accessible Computing
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
I began working on accessible computing in 2001 at the start of my doctoral program by developing word prediction software for Palm PDA devices [4]. Today, 25 years later, accessibility has remained a core focus of my work and the work of my students in the field of human-computer interaction (HCI). In this keynote, I will share five projects that have significantly shaped my work, along with five reflections that continue to inform my perspective. My goal is to convey ideas from which I would have benefitted 25 years ago as a junior researcher starting in accessible computing. My five projects are EdgeWrite [9], Slide Rule [3], enhanced area cursors [1] and, in particular, the Pointing Magnifier [2], ability-based design [7,8], and the epidemiological model of mobile app accessibility [5,6]. My five reflections concern prioritizing depth, the power of participant-driven prototyping, the opportunities and obligations of field deployments, the importance of conceptual contributions, and the value of cross-disciplinary deep-dives. I conclude by addressing some of the promises and pitfalls of artificial intelligence for accessibility, drawing on these reflections to light our way.

item.title: Designing and Evaluating an AI-Powered Figma Plugin for Accessibility Education
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Digital accessibility barriers are easier to prevent during design than to remediate after implementation, yet accessibility is often taught and practiced as a downstream concern. Despite growing attention in computing and design education, accessibility efforts continue to emphasize code-level auditing, remediation, and compliance checking, with less attention to early design decisions. The shift-left principle seeks to address this gap by embedding accessibility from the initial UX design phase, but its adoption remains limited. To explore how AI can support this shift, we developed a Figma plugin that uses a multimodal large language model (LLM) to evaluate UI frames against WCAG criteria and provide contextual, design-stage feedback. In a three-week deployment, 89 practicing professionals and computing or design students used the plugin alongside existing tools (Stark and Axe for Designers) and reported their perceptions, experiences, and self-reported abilities through pre- and post-use surveys. Overall, 92.1% reported identifying accessibility issues earlier, 96.6% reported productivity gains, and participants rated recommendation likelihood (M=4.25/5) and generated specification accuracy (M=4.08/5) highly. Findings also suggest that contextual AI feedback can help learners identify and reason about accessibility issues earlier in the design process. We conclude with practical takeaways for integrating AI-supported tools into accessibility education.

item.title: Zeno: Improving the Fidelity and Pedagogical Value of LLM-Generated Alt Text with BLV-Informed Guidelines and Iterative Prompting
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generating pedagogically useful alternative text (alt text) for advanced computer science course materials requires more than describing visual appearance: blind and low-vision learners often need descriptions that support tracing, comparison, equation reading, and task completion. This work-in-progress study examines how blind-learner-informed guidance can improve LLM-generated alt text for an online AI course. Inspired by a blind student’s longitudinal course experience, we introduce Delta, a CS-specific guideline for task-operable alt text, and Zeno, an iterative LLM workflow that generates, critiques, and revises alt text against the source material. In a formative evaluation with two sighted reviewers and one blind reviewer, Delta-informed prompting and Zeno substantially outperformed a WCAG-only baseline in sighted fidelity, pass rate, and diagnostic error patterns. These findings suggest that blind-learner-informed guidance can improve the pedagogical usefulness of LLM-generated alt text for technical course materials.

item.title: Learning Python as a Blind Programmer in an AI-Mediated Environment: An Autoethnographic Study
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Programming education is increasingly mediated by AI tools, yet little is known about how blind learners—particularly non-native English speakers—integrate these tools into learning, or where AI fails to address accessibility barriers. This paper presents an eight-week autoethnographic study of a blind, Chinese-speaking doctoral student learning introductory Python through Khan Academy’s curriculum with screen readers, a Braille display, and AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini). Drawing on detailed learning diaries and human–AI interaction logs analyzed via reflexive thematic analysis, we examine how AI mediates accessibility, cognition, and language during programming learning. Findings show that AI simultaneously functions as an accessibility interpreter, cognitive scaffold, and linguistic mediator, yet also introduces epistemic uncertainty, accessibility hallucinations, inconsistent cross-lingual terminology, and clear limits with non-textual cues. We argue that AI reconfigures rather than solves accessibility, and derive design implications for AI-assisted programming tools prioritizing explicit code structure, screen-reader integration, calibrated trust, and terminology-aware multilingual support.

item.title: Towards Accessible AI Literacy: Investigating How Teachers of Blind and Low-Vision Students Integrate Generative AI in Pedagogical Practices
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools are reshaping the educational landscape; yet, how teachers working with blind and low vision (BLV) students integrate these tools into their pedagogical practices remains underexplored. To address this gap, we interviewed 17 teachers of BLV students to investigate how they leverage GenAI to fulfill their teaching responsibilities and educate BLV students about these tools. We found that teachers incorporated GenAI for personalized lesson planning and tasks specific to BLV education, while counteracting biases favoring sighted teaching methods. They addressed BLV students’ curiosity and concerns about GenAI and taught them prompt formulation strategies that support their access needs in academic and daily tasks, although occasionally perpetuating their own misconceptions about GenAI to students. They expressed concerns about students’ overreliance on GenAI lowering foundational accessibility-related skills. We discuss ways to promote accessible AI literacy and outline design considerations for incorporating GenAI to support teachers’ BLV-specific instructional responsibilities and for integrating GenAI responsibly in BLV education.

item.title: A Recipe for Access: Visually Oriented Recipe Instructions as an Accessibility Barrier for Blind and Low-Vision Cooks
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
For people who are blind or have low vision (BLV), barriers to independent cooking are associated with reduced dietary quality and elevated health risks. One such barrier is embedded in recipe language itself: phrases such as “cook until golden brown” or “sauté until translucent” require visual monitoring. That such phrases exist is not new; what has been missing is evidence of their scale and an account of what BLV cooks do in their place. We use the term Visually Oriented Instructional Descriptor (VizOID) for this kind of recipe language. Across 573,986 recipes and 3.85 million instruction sentences, VizOIDs appeared in every corpus we examined, including 6.7% of instruction sentences and 35.9% of recipes overall, and 55.5% of recipes in the professionally written Food Network corpus. In a hand-labeled subset, independent human coders reached substantial agreement (κ = 0.730), and an LLM reached near-perfect post-adjudication agreement with human coding (κ = 0.961), showing that the phenomenon is detectable at scale. We then report semi-structured interviews with 12 BLV individuals to examine how they work through these instructions. Participants described a shared repertoire of non-visual cooking knowledge: timing as a proxy, smell, sound, touch, temperature, and familiar utensils used to infer food state. Framed through the social model of disability, our findings show that many recipes are inaccessible because recipe language fails to encode the non-visual knowledge BLV cooks already use. Our findings can inform vision rehabilitation therapists and AI accessibility researchers designing low-cost, language-level interventions that rewrite recipe text at the point of acquisition, grounded in BLV cooks’ lived expertise.

item.title: Prompting Change in the Welfare State: Co-designing an LLM-Assisted Toolkit of Welfare Stories and Tips with Aphasia Communities
item.description:
International ACM SIGACCESS Conference on Computers and Accessibility (ASSETS)
People with aphasia face substantial barriers when navigating digital welfare systems—including communication impairments, literacy demands and the cognitive burden of bureaucratic processes shaped by decades of austerity. We present Advokit, a multimodal AI toolkit co-designed with people with aphasia to support welfare navigation, application drafting and self-advocacy. Developed through a five-stage participatory design process, Advokit integrates accessible benefit information, a comparative benefits table, lived-experience stories and Benefit Buddy, an LLM-assisted drafting chatbot. Across a three-month real-world deployment, the toolkit recorded 800 visitors and 2,849 page views; users engaged most with the benefits table, benefits list and stories pages—reflecting demand for both structured guidance and peer-grounded narratives. Survey responses (n = 11) were broadly positive, particularly for information access, though Benefit Buddy onboarding scored lower. Analysis of 14 chatbot sessions showed the system excelled at translating established lived experience into application-ready language, but struggled when users first needed orientation before engaging with the drafting workflow. We frame Advokit as counter-infrastructure: a community-built response to the hostile design of the welfare system. Our findings also surface limitations of conversational AI interfaces as access mechanisms: as chatbots are increasingly deployed to mediate access to vital public services. We contribute an open-source co-designed welfare toolkit, empirical findings from its community deployment and design implications for accessible AI-supported public services.

item.title: Bounded Delegation: How Student Design Teams Keep Strategic Control over Generative AI
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
